extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing examiner practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and formulating determinations and rejections under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo test) including identification of judicial exceptions, assessment of additional elements (Step 2B), and use of streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use / technological environment limitations do not add an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely indicate a field of use or technological environment (e.g., limiting use to a particular industry, to the Internet, to a telephone network, or to a particular patient population) typically do no more than describe the environment in which a judicial exception is applied and therefore do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have characterized many such limitations as token or incidental additions that fail to integrate the judicial exception into the claim as a whole. Examples cited include limiting drug administration to certain patients (Mayo/Prometheus), identifying commodity providers/consumers (Bilski), limiting a formula to wheel circumference (Flook), specifying execution on a generic computer or Internet (FairWarning, Intellectual Ventures, buySAFE, Ultramercial), and limiting information collection/analysis to power grid data (Electric Power Group). Examiners should treat 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeably for eligibility analysis and consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)). When a limitation generally links a judicial exception to a particular environment, the examiner should explain why it does not meaningfully limit the claim (e.g., merely employing well-known computer functions to execute an abstract idea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of additional elements into the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional claim elements are integrated into the claim as a whole (i.e., act in concert with other limitations) or are merely incidental/token additions that do not alter how the claimed invention operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Diehr/Flook contrast: Diehr's specific, interrelated limitations (monitoring elapsed time, measuring temperature, repetitively calculating cure time, opening press automatically) were integrated and transformed a process, while Flook's catalytic chemical conversion limitation was incidental and not integrated. Integration that meaningfully transforms the claimed process can support eligibility; lack of integration suggests the limitation is a non-meaningful field-of-use or extra-solution activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) may be used when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may use a streamlined analysis when, viewed as a whole, the claim's eligibility is self-evident (for example, because the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The streamlined analysis (Pathway A) is for efficiency and yields the same result as the full Alice/Mayo analysis; it must not be used to avoid a finding of ineligibility that would occur under the full analysis. If there is doubt whether the applicant seeks coverage of a judicial exception, the full analysis should be conducted. The record may show eligibility simply by absence of an eligibility rejection or include clarifying remarks. Examples where streamlined analysis is appropriate: a robotic arm assembly with a control system operating using certain mathematical relationships, artificial hip prosthesis with a coating that does not tie up a nature-based product, or manufactured products with meaningful limitations that prevent tying up an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident when claim does not seek to tie up a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that does not attempt to tie up any judicial exception such that others cannot practice it may have self-evident eligibility and therefore not require full Alice/Mayo analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to complex manufactured industrial products/processes or products that merely include ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with gold contact, plastic chair with wood trim) can be self-evidently eligible. A claim that would be ineligible under Step 2B is not suitable for streamlined analysis. Use full analysis where the claims are a 'close call' (e.g., BASCOM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality avoids full Alice/Mayo analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to clear improvements in technology or computer functionality are not abstract when appropriately claimed and therefore may avoid full eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions (e.g., Enfish, McRO) support that claims demonstrating a tangible improvement to computer-related technology or other technological processes can be eligible at Step 2A (or allow Pathway A). If the improvement is clear, no further analysis may be needed. If it's a close call, perform the full analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate eligibility rejections based on substantive law and establish a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in substantive law under 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by judicial precedent and must set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility with sufficient clarity and specificity to notify the applicant and allow effective response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should review the entire record (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, prior art) and evaluate eligibility claim-by-claim. The initial burden is on the examiner to explain why a claim is ineligible. Training materials and examples do not themselves form the basis for rejection, though applicants may cite them in responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: When rejecting under Step 1, explain why claim is outside statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is determined not to fall within a statutory category (Step 1: NO), the rejection must explain why the claim is not directed to one of the four statutory categories of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 706.03(a) for making such a rejection. Provide sufficiently clear and specific reasoning in the Office action to enable applicant to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: When rejecting under Step 2A, identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The rejection must point to specific claim limitation(s) that recite or describe the judicial exception and explain why those limitations constitute an exception (e.g., an abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For abstract ideas, identify the idea as recited and explain why it corresponds to concepts courts have identified as abstract (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2)). Citing appropriate precedent that supports the identification is best practice; ensure cited decisions are factually applicable and avoid overreaching or relying on non-precedential decisions unless fact patterns match. For laws of nature/natural phenomena/product of nature, identify the recited subject matter and provide a reasoned rationale why it is such an exception (see MPEP § 2106.04(b) and § 2106.04(c)). Sample explanations are provided (e.g., claim recites sorting information by X similar to Digitech/Content Extraction; claim recites a correlation of X that is a law of nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: When rejecting under Step 2B, identify additional claim elements and explain why they do not amount to significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, the rejection must: (1) point to any additional elements beyond the exception, and (2) explain why these additional elements, individually and in combination, fail to add significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address the combination of elements as well as individual elements because a new combination may be patent eligible even if individual steps were known (Diamond v. Diehr). Where examiner concludes elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, explain why courts or skilled persons would so recognize them. Provide a reasoned explanation (not conclusory statements) supporting the conclusion that additional elements are conventional or fail to meaningfully limit the exception. Conversely, when appropriate, explain why additional elements do provide an inventive concept by adding meaningful limitations (see MPEP § 2106.05 and § 2106.07(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasoned rationale and factual tying when asserting abstract idea or conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not merely assert that claim language recites an abstract idea or conventional activity; explain with reasoned rationale and, where applicable, factual support how the claim language maps to the judicial exception or to well-understood, routine, conventional activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite applicable case law and tether the legal conclusion to the specific claim language and relevant facts in the record. Avoid reliance on language taken out of context and be cautious about citing non-precedential decisions unless the facts closely match the application under examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claims individually and consider dependent claims separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility should be evaluated claim-by-claim; dependent claims may add limitations that render them eligible even if the independent claim is ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume all claims with similar language stand or fall together. Each claim must be analyzed on the particular elements it recites, and dependent claims that add limitations may provide significantly more than the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Under compact prosecution, state all non-cumulative reasons for rejection in the first Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a §101 rejection is made, examiners should perform a complete examination for every claim under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting) and state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures that applicants receive a complete, efficient initial examination and supports prosecution procedure.
